Most studies have found no im- provement in progression-free or overall survival, and the general recommendation is that such extra therapy, with its associated toxicity, should not be used.1-5,8 This view has been challenged by a meta-analysis10 of 14 studies sug- gesting that there is evidence for benefit from maintenance therapy, although it is unclear which patients might benefit and which regimen would be most effective. Other strate- gies that have been tried, but with little consistent evidence of improved results, include the combination of irinotecan and cisplatin, the addition of further drugs to EP (such as ifosfamide, paclitaxel, or cyclophosphamide plus an an- thracycline), and the use of dose-intense or dose-dense regimens.1,5,8 Patients who have responded to initial treatment still have a more than 50% risk of developing brain metastases. Pro- phylactic cranial irradiation reduces this risk and improves survival in patients in complete remission.11 It is generally recommended for all patients with limited disease who achieve remission, and for those with extensive disease who achieve remission and have good prognostic factors and performance status.2-5,7,8 The value of chemotherapy in relapsed SCLC depends in part on the duration of remission before relapse, with greater responses the longer the remission.3,5,7,8 UK guide- lines recommend second-line chemotherapy only in pa- tients whose disease responded to first-line treatment.2 Pa- tients may be given the same initial therapy if they have relapsed after more than 6 months. Patients who relapse within 3 months of achieving remission are considered to have refractory disease; second-line drugs include ifosfa- mide, paclitaxel, docetaxel, and gemcitabine, although re- sponse is likely to be poor. Response rates are better if re- lapse occurs between 3 and 6 months after remission, and topotecan has been suggested as the best option. Other drugs that may be considered include irinotecan, gemcit- abine, a taxane, ifosfamide, oral etoposide, vinorelbine, or the CAV regimen.5,7,8 Drugs under investigation for SCLC include amrubicin, pemetrexed, and picoplatin.7,8 Second- line chemotherapy should be given until the patient re- ceives maximal benefit, becomes refractory, or develops unacceptable toxicity. Radiotherapy may also be given for localised symptomatic palliation.5 In patients with non-small cell lung cancer presenting with tumour localised to the lung (generally stage I and II), the treatment of choice is surgery.2,12-15 In patients with re- sectable disease who have medical contra-indications to surgery, radical radiotherapy is used with curative intent.
